extracted.intended_audience: inventors, mechanical engineers, and manufacturers planning new machinery or manufactories
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, testing, executing, and introducing mechanical inventions and for deciding when to apply machinery in manufacture. Covers estimating demand, experimental verification, working drawings, production economics, and organization of large establishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal communication for transplanting manufactures
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing but personal communication can enable our manufactures to be transplanted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the dolls' eyes anecdote: the author could not reproduce the article from description alone, but direct personal instruction from a practitioner enabled successful manufacture. Emphasises that practical, hands-on transmission is often essential when textual description fails to convey working methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate probable demand using empirical inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: In estimating sale of an article or the effects of a machine, empirical enquiry from competent persons and experiments should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a House of Commons committee first ascertained atmospheric deterioration of roads, then compared injury from horses' feet vs wheels using iron consumption data (Macneill's method). Use competent witnesses and measurable proxies to approximate demand/effects rather than relying on opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle for fair tolls on public roads
rubrics_metrics.description: The only ground on which a fair claim to toll can be made on any public road is to raise a fund, which, with the strictest economy, shall be just sufficient, first, to repay the expense of its original formation; secondly, to maintain it in good and sufficient repair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee used measured road injury to approximate just toll rates for steam-carriages. This is a normative standard for setting tolls based on full lifecycle cost recovery withEconomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider time-to-market and replacement dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: The time in which goods from a new factory can be brought to market and the time the new article will take to supersede those already in use should be well considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consumable goods (e.g., steel pens replacing quills) are more easily introduced than durable goods (e.g., locks). Even if a durable is cheaper or more secure, its adoption will be slow because old items are not rapidly removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate opposition from affected interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the opposition which the new manufacture may create by its real or apparent injury to other interests, and estimate the probable extent of its influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposition is often unforeseen or misestimated (example: steam-boats feared to ruin coaches but instead increased coach numbers). Evaluate political/social resistance and its likely (possibly temporary) effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make contrivance and improvements in drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: All the contrivance and all the improvements ought to be made in the drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For many mechanisms (if moderate power is the goal) the whole machine can be arranged on paper and proper strengths judged before construction. Emphasises thorough design documentation and use of drawings to identify improvements before fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct experiments for physical/chemical uncertainties
rubrics_metrics.description: There are circumstances dependent upon physical or chemical properties for which no drawings will be of any use — these are the legitimate objects of direct trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: punching letters into copper-plate — only experiments could determine burs, distortion, and plate behaviour. Conduct targeted physical trials to resolve effects not predictable from drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform experiments to verify manufacturability and side-effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment alone can determine difficulties such as burs from punching, distortion of neighbouring letters, interference with impressions, or plate deformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical testing revealed that right-angled punch sides produce negligible burs, depth sufficient for printing doesn't distort adjacent letters, burs can be scraped off, and plates remain fit to print. Use experiments to inform tolerances and process parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce most perfect working drawings before construction
rubrics_metrics.description: To make the most perfect drawings of every part tends essentially both to the success of the trial, and to economy in arriving at the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Execution from working drawings is relatively easy if good tools and methods are used. Good drawings reduce trial-and-error on the shop floor and enable predictable fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt workmanship and methods that reduce dependence on individual skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of working should be adopted in which the perfection of the part constructed depends less on the personal skill of the workmen than upon the certainty of the methods they employ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use jigs, tools, and standardized processes so that consistent quality is attainable by ordinary hands; rely on method and tooling rather than only on exceptional craftsmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for elasticity and support of parts in design
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglecting that metals are not perfectly rigid but elastic leads to errors; e.g., a small-diameter steel cylinder must be supported at proper intervals to act as an axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider elastic deformation, proper bearing supports, and framing stiffness. Failure to account for elasticity causes misalignment, friction, or failure in operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure stiff, immovable framing to preserve alignment and reduce friction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the bearings of the axis are once placed in a straight line they will continue so if the framing be immovable; if the framework changes form, even slightly, considerable friction will immediately arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stiff frame maintains alignment, reduces friction, and saves power. Example: in spinning districts it's estimated that fire-proof (rigid) buildings save about five percent on steam-engine power by preventing shaft misalignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept imperfect mechanical work for trials
rubrics_metrics.description: It is quite a mistaken idea to suppose that any imperfect mechanical work is good enough for a trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the experiment is worth trying, it should be tried with all the advantages of current mechanical art; imperfect trials may cause abandonment of viable ideas. Good initial workmanship prevents false negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat trials when the state of the art improves
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat, at the termination of intervals during which the art of making machinery has undergone any great improvement, the trials of methods which may have previously failed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some inventions failed only because contemporary manufacturing couldn't realize required tolerances. Re-test earlier ideas after general advances in tools and techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider full operational expense before construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the new or improved machine is intended to become the basis of a manufacture, it is essentially requisite that the whole expense attending its operations should be fully considered before its construction is undertaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate recurring costs, complexity-related expenses, and time-to-return. Complexity makes estimation harder. The first made unit often costs ~5 times the second due to setup, patterns, and drawing creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use division of labour and skilled draughtsmen
rubrics_metrics.description: The arts of contriving, of drawing, and of executing do not usually reside in their greatest perfection in one individual; the division of labour must be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a respectable draughtsman to help determine novelty and to produce working drawings. Specialists speed development and help avoid reinventing prior solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaust prior knowledge to verify novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertain whether the contrivance has the merit of novelty; examine with care the knowledge of contemporaries to avoid inventing again what has been better executed before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many projectors are negligent about prior art. Careful historical and technical survey prevents wasted effort and false claims of originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that invention is common but success requires perseverance
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of making new mechanical combinations is a possession common to a multitude of minds; the great success of eminent inventors was almost entirely due to unremitted perseverance and concentrated study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be misled by overconfidence; prepare for sustained effort and study rather than expect immediate triumph from a single idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply machinery when large numbers of identical items are required
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever it is required to produce a great multitude of things, all of exactly the same kind, the proper time has arrived for the construction of tools or machines by which they may be manufactured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economies of scale justify tooling and machinery (e.g., stocking-frames for many pairs; printing machinery for thousands of copies). If only a few items are needed, manual methods remain cheaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specialized tools even at increased expense when extreme accuracy or uniformity is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is required to produce a few articles — parts of machinery, for instance — which must be executed with the most rigid accuracy or be perfectly alike, it becomes nearly impossible to fulfil this condition without making tools expressly for the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept higher upfront cost for tooling if the required precision or interchangeability cannot be achieved by hand; tooling cost may exceed the value of the items but is justified by required tolerances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in machinery when time-to-produce critically affects value
rubrics_metrics.description: The shortness of time in which the article can be produced may have an important influence on its value and justify expensive machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New printing machines enabled newspapers to deliver timely news; hand-presses were too slow. Time-sensitive markets can justify greater capital expense for speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize factories to protect continuous, well-combined operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Large, skilfully arranged establishments require exclusion of visitors not from jealousy but from substantial inconvenience and loss of time caused by short interruptions to a series of well-combined operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protecting continuous workflows preserves output (example: The Times printing house where a quarter-hour interruption could cause loss of 1,000 copies). Plan layout and access policies to minimize interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider reducing transported mass and velocity for efficient letter conveyance
rubrics_metrics.description: In designing machinery for conveyance of letters it would be desirable to reduce the weight of matter to be conveyed with the letters and to reduce the velocity of the animal power employed, since faster driving reduces draw weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post-bag example: sending small mail weight with very heavy coaches is inefficient. Consider alternate mechanical systems (e.g., suspended wires, mechanical conveyances) if they satisfy constraints of weight, speed, and economy; some small-scale experiments may justify development.
